Federal law required openers made from January 1, 1991 to reverse on contact, and openers made from January 1, 1993 to add protection such as photo-eye sensors. It is the opener's age that matters, not the house's.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. of pre-1993 openers still in use.

check: Look for two small sensor 'eyes' about 6 inches off the floor on each side of the garage door opening.
Check the date on the opener's label.
Test it: lay a 2x4 flat on the floor under the door; the door should reverse when it touches the board.
garage-door-opener-no-auto-reverse.action: If the opener does not reverse or has no sensors, replace it with a current UL 325-compliant unit rather than trying to retrofit it. Until then, keep children clear of the door while it moves.
garage-door-opener-no-auto-reverse.caveat: The 1993 rule can be met by a constant-contact wall button instead of photo-eyes, so a newer opener without eyes is possible. Openers are often added or replaced long after a house is built.

non-safety-glazing-pre-1977.title: Non-tempered glass in doors and showers
non-safety-glazing-pre-1977.hook: Glass in doors, sliding patio doors and shower enclosures has had to be safety glass since July 1977, so older original glass may be ordinary glass that can cause serious cuts if someone falls through it.
non-safety-glazing-pre-1977.summary: A federal CPSC standard made safety glazing mandatory from July 6, 1977 in doors, storm doors, sliding glass doors, and tub and shower doors and enclosures. A house built before then that still has its original glass in those places may have ordinary annealed glass. Building codes later added other locations near doors, floors, stairs and tubs.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. of original pre-1977 glass still in place.

check: Look in each corner of the glass in doors, sliding doors and shower panels for a small etched or sandblasted mark naming the maker.
A mark reading 'tempered', '16 CFR 1201' or 'ANSI Z97.1' means safety glass.
No mark on a door or shower panel in an older house suggests ordinary glass.
non-safety-glazing-pre-1977.action: Replace unmarked glass in doors and showers with tempered or laminated safety glass, starting with the places people are most likely to fall against.
non-safety-glazing-pre-1977.caveat: Some states may have had their own safety-glazing laws earlier; that was not confirmed. Many doors and shower enclosures have been replaced since 1977.

residential-fire-sprinklers.title: Home fire sprinklers
residential-fire-sprinklers.hook: California has required fire sprinklers in new one- and two-family homes since 2011, so newer California houses generally have small sprinkler heads in the ceilings.
residential-fire-sprinklers.summary: A model code change requiring sprinklers in new one- and two-family homes took effect January 1, 2011. California adopted it statewide; Pennsylvania adopted it and repealed it the same year. Sprinklers need little care, but painted or blocked heads must be replaced and the control valve must stay open.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: California has required sprinklers in all new residential construction since 2011 (Wikipedia). Outside places that require them, they are uncommon in houses.

check: Look up: small sprinkler heads, often under flat white cover plates, in the ceiling of every room.
Find the riser, a pipe with a gauge and flow switch, near the water main or in the garage.
residential-fire-sprinklers.action: Keep the control valve open and never paint over a sprinkler head. Replace any head that has been painted or blocked.
residential-fire-sprinklers.caveat: Some cities outside California also require sprinklers by local ordinance. Houses permitted before 2011 but finished later may not have them.

buried-heating-oil-tank.reason: Depends on the exact address (whether the property was ever on oil heat), and no source dates residential installation.

carbon-monoxide-alarms.reason: Unconfirmed: the 2009 IRC requirement could not be verified.

bedroom-egress-windows.reason: Unconfirmed: no verified source for any code date.

guard-baluster-spacing.reason: Unconfirmed: every historical date is unverified.

unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.title: House not bolted to its foundation
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.hook: Many older West Coast houses on crawl spaces are not adequately bolted to their foundations, and in a strong earthquake they can slide off.
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.summary: Older wood-frame houses on raised foundations often have the wooden sill plate sitting on the concrete without enough anchor bolts, and short 'cripple' walls with no bracing. In strong shaking the house can shift off its foundation. Bolting the sill and sheathing the cripple walls with plywood is the standard retrofit.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Only houses on raised foundations with crawl spaces are affected; slab houses are not.

check: Go into the crawl space and look along the top of the concrete foundation at the wooden sill plate.
Bolts with nuts and washers every 4 to 6 feet mean it is bolted.
If there is a short wood-stud wall between the foundation and the floor, check whether plywood or OSB is nailed to its inside face.
Houses on a concrete slab have no cripple wall.
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.action: A contractor can bolt the sill and brace the cripple walls following your state's or city's prescriptive retrofit plans; taller cripple walls need an engineer. In California, check whether a state grant program covers your ZIP code.
unbolted-foundation-unbraced-cripple-wal.caveat: There is no single code year: a reference source says many houses built before 1950 lack adequate bolting, and the pre-1980 cutoff used in California is a grant-program screen, not a code date. Many houses have already been retrofitted.

unreinforced-masonry-urm.title: Unreinforced brick (URM) houses
unreinforced-masonry-urm.hook: Along Utah's Wasatch Front, many solid-brick houses built before 1975 have no steel reinforcement, and FEMA counts over 185,000 such buildings in the Salt Lake Valley alone.
unreinforced-masonry-urm.summary: Unreinforced masonry walls can crack and fall in an earthquake, and parapets and chimneys tend to go first. In Utah, codes for new buildings began addressing this in 1975, and many unreinforced buildings there are single-family houses. Tying walls to floors and roof and bracing chimneys are the usual retrofits.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: FEMA P-774: over 185,000 unreinforced masonry buildings in the Salt Lake Valley alone, many of them single-family homes.

check: Look at the outside brick walls: a row of bricks laid end-on (a header course) every 5 to 7 rows means solid brick, not veneer.
At a window opening, walls 8 to 13 inches thick point to solid masonry.
Star-shaped or square metal plates on the outside wall show past retrofit ties.
Brick veneer over a wood frame has no header rows and is a different, lesser issue.
unreinforced-masonry-urm.action: Have a structural engineer assess it. Salt Lake City has run a 'Fix the Bricks' program that helps pay for roof-to-wall ties and chimney bracing; check whether it covers your house.
unreinforced-masonry-urm.caveat: Shown for Utah, where the 1975 date is confirmed. California, Oregon and Washington also have unreinforced brick buildings with earlier cutoffs (California's seismic codes began in the 1930s), but most of those are commercial or apartment buildings.

florida-pre-2002-wind-construction.title: Florida home built before the statewide wind code
florida-pre-2002-wind-construction.hook: Florida homes permitted before March 1, 2002 were built to local codes rather than the statewide Florida Building Code that followed Hurricane Andrew.
florida-pre-2002-wind-construction.summary: After Hurricane Andrew, South Florida created High-Velocity Hurricane Zones in its 1994 code, and the statewide Florida Building Code took effect March 1, 2002. Older homes may have roofs held to the walls only by nails rather than metal straps, and no protection over windows and doors. A wind-mitigation inspection documents what a house actually has.

prevalence.label: likely
prevalence.note: Wikipedia: about 4.7 million Florida homes predate the modern Florida Building Code.

check: In the attic at the eaves, look where each truss or rafter meets the top of the wall.
Only angled nails means toe-nailed; a small metal bracket is a clip; a metal strap wrapping over the truss is a wrap, and two straps a double wrap.
Check windows and doors for impact-rated labels or shutter hardware.
Your county permit record gives the original permit date.
florida-pre-2002-wind-construction.action: Get a wind-mitigation inspection by a licensed inspector; it records these features for your insurer. Upgrades such as roof-to-wall straps, re-nailing the roof deck and shutters are usually done at re-roofing time.
florida-pre-2002-wind-construction.caveat: What counts is the permit application date, not the year the house was finished, so 2002 houses can go either way. In Miami-Dade and Broward the stricter code dates from 1994. Many pre-2002 homes do have clips or straps.

pyrrhotite-crumbling-foundations.title: Crumbling concrete foundations (pyrrhotite)
pyrrhotite-crumbling-foundations.hook: In parts of north-central Connecticut and central Massachusetts, some foundations poured with local quarry stone are crumbling because of a mineral called pyrrhotite.
pyrrhotite-crumbling-foundations.summary: NIST says damage to concrete in central Connecticut has been attributed to pyrrhotite, an iron sulfide mineral in the aggregate. State officials use 1983 to 2015 as the window for affected foundations, and cracking usually appears 10 to 30 years after construction. The fix is replacing the foundation, which is a major job.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Estimates of affected homes vary by two orders of magnitude, and the risk is limited to certain towns; outside them it is essentially nil.

check: In the basement, look at the foundation walls for horizontal cracks and map-pattern (spider-web) cracking.
Look for white powdery deposits, rust-brown staining and flaking.
A clean-looking wall does not rule it out; a licensed engineer's visual inspection and a core sample tested for pyrrhotite confirm it.
pyrrhotite-crumbling-foundations.action: If you are in an affected town, have a licensed engineer inspect the foundation, especially before buying. Connecticut and Massachusetts have run programs for testing, and Connecticut for repairs; check what is currently available.
pyrrhotite-crumbling-foundations.caveat: The 1983 to 2015 window comes from state officials' figures that could not be independently confirmed, and only towns near the source quarries are affected. Most houses in Connecticut and Massachusetts are not at risk.

engineered-i-joists-fire.title: Engineered I-joist floors
engineered-i-joists-fire.hook: By 2005 about half of new wood floors were built on engineered I-joists, which perform well day to day but can fail quickly in a fire if left exposed.
engineered-i-joists-fire.summary: I-joists, invented in 1969, have a thin OSB or plywood web between small top and bottom flanges. Their known drawback is very rapid failure when directly exposed to fire, which matters over an unfinished basement or garage with no ceiling. Covering the underside with drywall is the usual protection.

prevalence.label: possible
prevalence.note: Wikipedia: about 50% of wood light-frame floors used I-joists as of 2005.

check: Look up at the basement or garage ceiling for I-shaped joists: a thin OSB or plywood web with small lumber flanges top and bottom.
They are usually printed with a brand such as TJI, BCI or LPI.
If you can see them, they are unprotected from below.
engineered-i-joists-fire.action: Consider covering exposed I-joists with 1/2-inch drywall, and make sure working smoke alarms cover every level, including the basement.
engineered-i-joists-fire.caveat: A model-code requirement to cover them was reportedly added around 2012, but that was not confirmed and states adopted it unevenly. The hazard applies only where the joists are exposed.

roof-trusses-metal-plate.title: Factory-built roof trusses
roof-trusses-metal-plate.hook: If your attic is a web of diagonal 2x4s joined by toothed metal plates, the roof is built from factory trusses, and cutting even one can badly weaken it.
roof-trusses-metal-plate.summary: Metal-plate-connected roof trusses date from the mid-1950s and became a common way to frame roofs. They are efficient, but every piece carries load. Cutting or altering a truss, for attic storage, a skylight or ductwork, needs an engineer's repair design.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. for houses by year built.

check: In the attic, look for diagonal 2x4s forming W or M shapes, joined by toothed galvanized steel plates, usually 24 inches apart.
Rafters, by contrast, are larger boards running from the ridge to the wall with open space between.
Look for cut or notched members and plates that have backed out of the wood.
roof-trusses-metal-plate.action: Nothing is needed unless trusses are damaged or altered. Before any attic conversion, skylight or other change that touches a truss, get an engineer's design.
roof-trusses-metal-plate.caveat: Truss use grew over decades, and many houses still use rafters, especially custom homes and complex roofs. Sources date the connector plate to 1952 or 1955.

pre-1976-mobile-homes.title: Mobile home built before the HUD Code
pre-1976-mobile-homes.hook: Mobile homes made before June 15, 1976 predate the federal HUD Code and cannot get FHA-insured mortgages.
pre-1976-mobile-homes.summary: Every manufactured home built after June 15, 1976 carries a HUD certification label and meets federal construction and safety standards. Earlier units were built before those standards, and HUD does not issue labels for them. This matters only if your home is a manufactured (mobile) home.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. of surviving pre-1976 units. Every mobile home made before the date predates the HUD Code by definition.

check: Look for a metal certification label, about 2 by 4 inches, riveted to the outside at the tail end of each section.
Look for a paper data plate inside, often in a kitchen cabinet, the electrical panel or a bedroom closet, giving the manufacture date.
No label and no data plate, plus a title showing a pre-1976 year, means pre-HUD Code.
pre-1976-mobile-homes.action: It cannot be certified after the fact. Focus on safety upgrades such as smoke alarms, a wiring evaluation and tie-downs. Expect financing limits: FHA does not insure mortgages on these homes.
pre-1976-mobile-homes.caveat: The date is when the home left the factory, not its model year or when it was placed, so a '1976' home can fall on either side.

manufactured-homes-pre-1994-wind-zones.title: Manufactured home built before 1994 wind standards
manufactured-homes-pre-1994-wind-zones.hook: After Hurricane Andrew, HUD raised the wind standards for manufactured homes made from July 13, 1994, with zones designed for 100 and 110 mph winds.
manufactured-homes-pre-1994-wind-zones.summary: Manufactured homes made before July 13, 1994 were built to the older wind standard. The newer rule created Wind Zones II and III for hurricane-prone areas. This matters only for manufactured homes, and most of all on the hurricane coast.

prevalence.label: unknown
prevalence.note: No reliable count exists. Every manufactured home made before the date was built to the older standard.

check: Find the data plate inside the home, often in a kitchen cabinet, the electrical panel or a bedroom closet.
Read the manufacture date and the wind-zone map showing which zone (I, II or III) the home was designed for.
No wind-zone designation, or a date before July 1994, means the older standard.
manufactured-homes-pre-1994-wind-zones.action: Have the anchoring and tie-downs checked and brought up to current installation standards. Only replacement gets you the post-1994 structural design.
manufactured-homes-pre-1994-wind-zones.caveat: Date of manufacture governs, not the year the home was placed. Exactly which counties fall in each wind zone was not confirmed; the higher zones cover the hurricane coast.

soft-story-wood-frame-apartments.reason: Depends on the exact address and building type: applies to multi-unit apartment buildings covered by specific California city ordinances, not to houses by year and state.

hurricane-straps-gulf-atlantic.reason: Unconfirmed: no verified source for any state date.

pre-firm-flood-construction.reason: Depends on the exact address: whether the lot is in a mapped flood zone and the date of that community's first flood map.

texas-expansive-clay-slab-foundations.reason: Unconfirmed, and there is no cut-off year; soil, not build year, drives it.

stone-brick-rubble-foundations.reason: Unconfirmed: the 1940 end year and all prevalence are unsourced.

permanent-wood-foundations.reason: Too weak: rare (over 300,000 structures, trade source) and build year only rules out houses before about 1971.

california-chapter-7a-wildfire.reason: Unconfirmed (the 2008 date could not be verified), and it depends on whether the exact parcel is in a mapped fire hazard zone.

snow-load-older-roofs.reason: Too weak: no cut-off year exists (codes changed across the 1970s and 1980s) and the guidance targets larger, flatter buildings.

termite-wood-soil-contact.reason: No dated code milestone verified; build year does not predict it.
